READING 5
STATISTICAL CHARACTERISTICS
OF ASSET RETURNS
MODULE 5.1: MEASURES OF CENTRAL
TENDENCY
LOS 5.a: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate various measures of (1) central
tendency and location and (2) dispersion.
Measures of central tendency identify the center, or average, of a dataset. This
central point can then be used to represent the typical, or expected, value.
Two concepts are important here: the population and the sample. The
population represents the entire set of data points or elements that can be
observed, such as the entire history of percentage changes in the price of oil. A
sample is a subset of a population, such as percentage changes in the price of oil
over the last five years.
The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observed values divided by the number
of observations. It is the most widely used measure of central tendency. An
example of an arithmetic mean is a sample mean, which is the sum of all the
values in a sample, divided by the number of observations in the sample, n. It is
used to make inferences about the population mean.
The sample mean is:
The population mean is:

The median is the midpoint of a dataset when the data is arranged in ascending
or descending order. Half of the observations lie above the median, and half are
below. To determine the median, arrange the data from the highest to lowest
value, or lowest to highest value, and find the middle observation (if the dataset
has an odd number of observations) or the average of the middle two
observations (if the dataset has an even number of observations).
EXAMPLE: Median using an odd number of observations
What is the median return for five portfolio managers with a 10-year
annualized total returns record of 30%, 15%, 25%, 21%, and 23%?
Answer:
First, arrange the returns in descending (or ascending) order:
30%, 25%, 23%, 21%, 15%
Then, select the observation that has an equal number of observations above
and below it—the one in the middle. For this dataset, the third observation,
23%, is the median.
EXAMPLE: Median using an even number of observations
Suppose we add a sixth manager to the previous example with a return of 28%.
What is the median return?
Answer:
Arranging the returns in descending order gives us this:
30%, 28%, 25%, 23%, 21%, 15%
With an even number of observations, there is no single middle value. The
median value, in this case, is the arithmetic mean of the two middle
observations, 25% and 23%. Thus, the median return for the six managers 
The median is important because the arithmetic mean can be affected by
outliers, which are extremely large or small values. When this occurs, the
median is a better measure of central tendency than the mean because it is not
affected by extreme values that might result from measurement error, data entry
error, sampling errors, or simply from the actual variability of the data.

Consider the sample data: 12%, 14%, 16%, 17%, and 19%, for which the mean
is 15.6% and the median is 16%. If we replace 19% with an outlier value of
30%, the median is unchanged at 16%, while the mean is increased to 17.8%.
When a statistical estimate produces reliable results in the presence of outliers,
or when the data are from a different distribution than the researcher has
assumed, we refer to it as a robust estimator. The median is a more robust
estimator of central tendency than the mean.
The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a dataset. A dataset may
have more than one mode, or no mode. The dataset 1, 1, 1, 3, 5, 6, 6, 6 has two
modes, 1 and 6, and is referred to as bimodal.
EXAMPLE: Mode
What is the mode of the following dataset?
Dataset: [30%, 28%, 25%, 23%, 28%, 15%, 5%]
Answer:
The mode is 28% because it is the value appearing most frequently.
For continuous data, such as investment returns, we typically do not identify a
single outcome as the mode. Instead, we divide the relevant range of outcomes
into intervals, and we identify the modal interval as the one into which the
largest number of observations fall.
Methods for Dealing With Outliers
In some cases, a researcher may decide that outliers should be excluded from a
measure of central tendency. One technique for doing so is to use a trimmed
mean. A trimmed mean excludes a stated percentage of the most extreme
observations. A 1% trimmed mean, for example, would discard the lowest 0.5%
and the highest 0.5% of the observations.
Another technique is to use a winsorized mean. With a winsorized mean,
instead of discarding the highest and lowest observations, we substitute values
for them. To calculate a 90% winsorized mean, for example, we would
determine the 5th and 95th percentile of the observations, substitute the 5th
percentile value for any values lower than that, substitute the 95th percentile

value for any values higher than that, and then calculate the mean of the revised
dataset. Percentiles are measures of location, and we address them next.
Quantiles
Quantile is the general term for a value at or below which a stated proportion of
the data in a distribution lies.
Examples of quantiles include the following:
Quartile. The distribution is divided into quarters.
Quintile. The distribution is divided into fifths.
Decile. The distribution is divided into tenths.
Percentile. The distribution is divided into hundredths (percentages).
Any quantile may be expressed as a percentile. For example, the third quartile
partitions a distribution such that three-fourths, or 75%, of the observations fall
below that value. Thus, the third quartile is the 75th percentile. The difference
between the third quartile and the first quartile (25th percentile) is known as the
interquartile range.
To visualize a dataset, we can create a box and whisker plot, as shown in Figure
5.1. In a box and whisker plot, the box represents the central portion of the data,
such as the interquartile range. The vertical line represents the entire range. In
Figure 5.1, we can see that the largest observation is farther away from the
center than the smallest observation. This suggests that the data might include
one or more outliers on the upper end.
Figure 5.1: Box and Whisker Plot

If the data are measured correctly (no data errors), it may be best to include all
data values, so as not to discard any valid data points and reflect the
characteristics of the distribution accurately. Trimming the data by discarding
upper and lower values offers an objective identification of which observations
are considered outliers, but it may remove valuable information about the
distribution. Winsorizing the data, replacing high and low outliers with
percentile values, preserves more information than a trimmed mean. With a
small number of outliers, the winsorized mean will be a better measure of a
distribution’s central tendency than either an arithmetic mean or a trimmed
mean.
Statistical analysis works best when data are stationary, with a mean and
variance of the underlying distribution that do not change over time. When the
characteristics of a distribution vary over time, the distribution is termed
nonstationary, making statistical analysis and tests less reliable.
As an example, a price series that increases over time, such as stock prices or
index values, is nonstationary. If we instead examine weekly or monthly
percentage changes in prices, we may find that the distribution of the data is
stationary over longer time periods.

MODULE 5.2: DISPERSION, SKEWNESS, AND
KURTOSIS
Dispersion is defined as variability around the central tendency. The common
theme in finance and investments is the tradeoff between reward and risk, where
central tendency of returns is the measure of reward and dispersion of returns is
the measure of risk.
The range is a relatively simple measure of variability, but when used with other
measures, it provides useful information. The range is the distance between the
largest and the smallest value in a dataset.
range = maximum value − minimum value
EXAMPLE: Range
What is the range for the 5-year annualized total returns for five investment
managers if the managers’ individual returns were 30%, 12%, 25%, 20%, and
23%?
Answer:
range = 30 − 12 = 18%
The mean absolute deviation (MAD) is the average of the absolute values of
the deviations of individual observations from the arithmetic mean.
The reason MAD uses absolute values of each deviation is because the sum of
actual deviations from the arithmetic mean is always zero.

EXAMPLE: Mean absolute deviation
What is the MAD of the investment returns for the five managers discussed in
the preceding example? How is it interpreted?
Answer:

This result can be interpreted to mean that, on average, an individual return
will deviate ±4.8% from the mean return of 22%.
Another measure of dispersion is the median absolute deviation, which is the
median of the absolute deviations from the data’s median:
median absolute deviation = Med(|Xi − Med(X)|)
Compared to the MAD, the median absolute deviation is a more robust measure
of dispersion.
Variance and Standard Deviation
The two most widely used measures of dispersion, variance and standard
deviation, are based on squared deviations from the mean.
Population variance, σ2, is defined as the average of the squared deviations
around the population mean, μ:
The variance calculation squares the deviations around the mean to resolve the
problem that the sum of negative and positive deviations is always zero. The
variance of financial asset returns measures the variability of the asset returns,
with a higher variance indicating greater risk. Variance is sensitive to outliers
because squaring the deviations magnifies the importance of outliers.

Population standard deviation, σ, is the positive square root of the population
variance:
Unlike variance, standard deviation is in the same units as the original data (e.g.,
percentage returns, dollars, euros), rather than those units squared.
The sample variance, s2, is the measure of dispersion that applies when we are
evaluating a sample of n observations from a population. Sample variance is
calculated using the following formula:
The denominator for s2 is n − 1, one less than the sample size n. Based on
statistical theory, using the entire number of sample observations, n, instead of n
− 1, as the divisor in the computation of s2, would systematically underestimate
the population variance—particularly for smaller sample sizes. This systematic
underestimation causes the sample variance to be a biased estimator of the
population variance. Using n − 1 instead of n in the denominator (an adjustment
known as Bessel’s correction) improves the statistical properties of s2 as an
estimator of the population variance.

In statistical theory, the root of time law holds that variance increases linearly
with time. For example, if the variance of daily returns is σ2, the variance of
weekly returns is 5 × σ2. Because we would calculate standard deviation of daily
returns as the square root of σ2 = σ, the standard deviation of weekly returns is
the square root of (5 × σ2), which equals 
 However, this relation does not
always hold in practice. The variance of returns for longer time periods tends to
be less than predicted by statistical theory, because of differences between the
characteristics of the observed data and the assumptions underlying the theory.
LOS 5.b: Describe, interpret, and evaluate measures of skewness and
kurtosis.

A distribution is symmetrical if it is shaped identically on both sides of its mean.
Distributional symmetry implies that intervals of losses and gains will exhibit
the same frequency. For example, a symmetrical distribution with a mean return
of zero will have losses in the −6% to −4% interval as frequently as it will have
gains in the +4% to +6% interval. The extent to which a returns distribution is
symmetrical is important because the degree of symmetry tells analysts whether
deviations from the mean are more likely to be above it or below it.
Skewness, or skew, refers to the extent to which a distribution is not
symmetrical. Nonsymmetrical distributions may be either positively or
negatively skewed and result from the occurrence of outliers in the dataset.
A positively skewed distribution is characterized by outliers greater than the
mean (in the upper region, or right tail). A positively skewed distribution is
said to be “skewed right” because of its relatively long upper (right) tail.
A negatively skewed distribution has a disproportionately large number of
outliers less than the mean that fall within its lower (left) tail. A negatively
skewed distribution is said to be “skewed left” because of its long lower tail.
Skewness affects the location of the mean, median, and mode of a distribution:
For a symmetrical distribution, the mean, median, and mode are equal.
For a positively skewed, unimodal distribution, the mode is less than the
median, which is less than the mean. The mean is affected by outliers; a
positively skewed distribution has large positive outliers, which will tend to
pull the mean upward, or more positive.
For a negatively skewed, unimodal distribution, the mean is less than the
median, which is less than the mode. In this case, large negative outliers tend to
pull the mean downward (to the left).
An example of a positively skewed distribution is that of housing prices.
Suppose you live in a neighborhood with 100 homes: 99 of them sell for
$100,000, and one sells for $1,000,000. The median and the mode will be
$100,000, but the mean will be $109,000. Hence, the mean has been pulled
upward (to the right) by the existence of one expensive home (outlier) in the
neighborhood.
The key to remembering how measures of central tendency are affected by
skewed data is to recognize that skew affects the mean more than the median and

mode, and the mean is pulled in the direction of the skew. The relative location
of the mean, median, and mode for different distribution shapes is shown in
Figure 5.2. Note that the median is between the other two measures for both
positively and negatively skewed distributions.

PROFESSOR’S NOTE
The LOS requires us to “describe, interpret, and evaluate” measures of
skewness and kurtosis, but not to calculate them.
When a distribution is right skewed, sample skewness is positive because the
deviations above the mean are larger, on average. A left-skewed distribution has
a negative sample skewness. If skewness is equal to zero, the distribution is
symmetrical.
Kurtosis is a measure of the degree to which a distribution is more or less
peaked than a normal distribution (which we will describe in our next reading).
Leptokurtic describes a distribution that is more peaked than a normal
distribution, whereas platykurtic refers to a distribution that is less peaked, or
flatter, than a normal one. A distribution is mesokurtic if it has the same kurtosis
as a normal distribution.
As indicated in Figure 5.3, a leptokurtic return distribution will have more
returns clustered around the mean (more peaked) and more returns with large
deviations from the mean (fatter tails). Relative to a normal distribution, a
leptokurtic distribution will have a greater percentage of small deviations from
the mean and a greater percentage of extremely large deviations from the mean.
This means that there is a relatively greater probability of an observed value
being either close to the mean or far from the mean. Regarding an investment
returns distribution, a greater likelihood of a large deviation from the mean
return is often perceived as an increase in risk.
Figure 5.3: Kurtosis

Kurtosis is calculated as follows:
A distribution is said to exhibit excess kurtosis if it has more or less kurtosis
than a normal distribution. The kurtosis of a normal distribution equals three.
Statisticians, however, sometimes report excess kurtosis, which is defined as
kurtosis minus three. Thus, a normal distribution has excess kurtosis equal to
zero, a leptokurtic distribution has excess kurtosis greater than zero, and a
platykurtic distribution has excess kurtosis less than zero.
Kurtosis is critical in a risk management setting. Most research about the
distribution of securities returns has shown that returns are not normally
distributed. Actual securities returns tend to exhibit both skewness and kurtosis.
When securities returns are modeled using an assumed normal distribution,
predictions from the models will not consider the potential for extremely large
negative outcomes. In fact, most risk managers put little emphasis on the mean
and standard deviation of a distribution and focus more on the distribution of
returns in the tails of the distribution, because that is where the risk is. In
general, greater excess kurtosis and more negative skew in returns distributions
indicate increased risk.

MODULE 5.3: COVARIANCE, CORRELATION,
AND ALTERNATIVE MEASURES OF
DISPERSION
LOS 5.c: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate covariance and correlation.
Scatter plots are a method for displaying the relationship between two variables.
With one variable on the vertical axis and the other on the horizontal axis, their
paired observations can each be plotted as a single point. For example, in Panel
A of Figure 5.4, the point farthest to the upper right shows that when one of the
variables (on the horizontal axis) equaled 9.2, the other variable (on the vertical
axis) equaled 8.5.
The scatter plot in Panel A is typical of two variables that have no clear
relationship. Panel B shows two variables that have a strong linear relationship.
As we will see shortly, this implies that these variables exhibit a high correlation
coefficient.
A key advantage of creating scatter plots is that they can reveal nonlinear
relationships, which are not described by the correlation coefficient. Panel C
illustrates such a relationship. Although the correlation coefficient for these two
variables is close to zero, their scatter plot shows clearly that they are related in a
predictable way.

In practice, covariance is difficult to interpret. The value of covariance depends
on the units of the variables. For example, the covariance of daily price changes
of two securities priced in yen will be much greater than their covariance if the
securities are priced in dollars. Like the variance, the units of covariance are the
square of the units used for the data.
Additionally, we cannot interpret the relative strength of the relationship between
two variables using their covariance. Knowing that the covariance of X and Y is
0.8756 tells us only that they tend to move together, because the covariance is
positive.
A standardized measure of the linear relationship between two variables is called
the correlation coefficient, or simply correlation. The correlation between two
variables, X and Y, is calculated as follows:
The properties of the correlation of two random variables, X and Y, are
summarized here:
Correlation measures the strength of the linear relationship between two
random variables.
Correlation has no units; it is a scale-free measure.
Possible values of the correlation coefficient range from −1 to +1. That is, −1 ≤
ρXY ≤ +1.
If ρXY = 1.0, the random variables have perfect positive correlation. This
indicates that a movement in one random variable relative to its mean results in
a proportional positive movement in the other relative to its mean.
If ρXY = −1.0, the random variables have perfect negative correlation. This
indicates that a movement in one random variable relative to its mean results in
an exact opposite proportional movement in the other relative to its mean.
If ρXY = 0, there is no linear relationship between the variables, indicating that
a prediction of Y cannot be made on the basis of X using linear methods.
EXAMPLE: Correlation

The variance of returns on Stock A is 0.0028, the variance of returns on Stock
B is 0.0124, and their covariance of returns is 0.0058. Calculate and interpret
the correlation of the returns for Stocks A and B.
Answer:
First, it is necessary to convert the variances to standard deviations:
sA = (0.0028)½ = 0.0529
sB = (0.0124)½ = 0.1114
Now, the correlation between the returns of Stock A and Stock B can be
computed as follows:
The fact that this value is close to +1 indicates that the linear relationship is not
only positive, but also very strong.
Analysts should take care when drawing conclusions based on correlation.
Causation is not implied simply from significant correlation. Even if it were,
correlation does not reveal which variable is driving change in the other. It is
more prudent to say that two variables exhibit positive (or negative) association,
suggesting that the nature of any causal relationship is to be investigated
separately or based on theory that can be subject to additional tests.
One question that can be investigated is the role of outliers in the correlation of
two variables. If removing the outliers reduces the calculated correlation
significantly, further inquiry is necessary into whether the outliers provide
information or are caused by noise (randomness) in the data used.
Spurious correlation refers to correlation that is either the result of chance or
present due to changes in both variables over time that is caused by their
association with a third variable. For example, we can find instances where two
variables that are both related to the inflation rate exhibit significant correlation,
but for which causation in either direction is not present.
In his book Spurious Correlation,1 Tyler Vigen presents the following examples.
The correlation between the age of each year’s Miss America and the number of
films Nicolas Cage appeared in that year is 87%. This seems a bit random. The
correlation between the United States spending on science, space, and

technology and suicides by hanging, strangulation, and suffocation over the
1999–2009 period is 99.87%. It is an impressive correlation, but both variables
increased in an approximately linear fashion over the period.
LOS 5.d: Calculate, interpret, and evaluate semi-deviation and coefficient of
variation.
When we use variance or standard deviation as risk measures, we calculate risk
based on outcomes both above and below the mean. In some situations, it may
be more appropriate to consider only outcomes less than the mean (or some
other specific value) when calculating a risk measure. In this case, we are
measuring downside risk.
The semivariance is the variance of only those outcomes below the mean,
calculated as follows:
A related measure of downside risk is target downside deviation, which is also
known as target semideviation. Calculating target downside deviation is similar
to calculating standard deviation—but in this case, we choose a target value
against which to measure each outcome and only include deviations if the
outcomes are below that target.

using all the observations in the numerator.

A direct comparison between two or more measures of dispersion may be
difficult. For instance, suppose you are comparing the annual returns distribution
for retail stocks with a mean of 8% and an annual returns distribution for a real
estate portfolio with a mean of 16%. Comparing the dispersions of the two
distributions directly is not meaningful because of the relatively large difference
in their means. To make a meaningful comparison, we must use a relative
measure of dispersion. Relative dispersion is the amount of variability in a
distribution around a reference point or benchmark.
Relative dispersion is commonly measured with the coefficient of variation
(CV), which is computed as follows:
CV measures the amount of dispersion in a distribution relative to its mean. This
is useful because it enables us to compare dispersion across different sets of data.
In an investment setting, the CV is used to measure the risk (variability) per unit
of expected return (mean). A lower CV is better.
EXAMPLE: Coefficient of variation
During an observed period of time, the mean monthly return on T-bills is
0.25% with a standard deviation of 0.36%, and the mean monthly return for the
S&P 500 is 1.09% with a standard deviation of 7.30%. Calculate and interpret
the CV for these two investments.

Answer:
These results indicate that there is less dispersion (risk) per unit of monthly
return for T-bills than for the S&P 500 (1.44 vs. 6.70).

KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 5.a

The arithmetic mean is the average of observations. The sample mean is the
arithmetic mean of sample data.
The median is the midpoint of a dataset when the data is arranged in order.
The mode of a dataset is the value (or values) that occur most frequently. The
modal interval is a measure of mode for continuous data.
A trimmed mean omits outliers. A winsorized mean replaces outliers with given
values. Both reduce the effect of outliers on the mean.
A quartile divides a distribution into quarters. A percentile divides a distribution
into hundredths (percentages). The interquartile range is the difference between
the 75th and 25th percentiles; it represents the central 50% of the data.
The range is the difference between the largest and smallest values in a dataset.
Mean absolute deviation is the average of the absolute values of the deviations
from the arithmetic mean.
Variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the arithmetic mean.
Standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance, and it is frequently
used as a measure of risk.
LOS 5.b
Skewness describes the degree to which a distribution deviates from symmetry.
Zero skew indicates symmetry around a central value. Right or positive skew
indicates more outcomes in the upper part of the distribution. Left or negative
skew indicates the opposite. For a positively skewed, unimodal distribution, the
mean is greater than the median, which is greater than the mode. For a
negatively skewed, unimodal distribution, the mean is less than the median,
which is less than the mode.
Kurtosis measures the peakedness of a distribution and the probability of
extreme outcomes (thickness of tails). Excess kurtosis is measured relative to the
shape of a normal distribution, which has a kurtosis of 3. Positive excess kurtosis
indicates a distribution that has fatter tails than a normal distribution. Negative
excess kurtosis indicates thinner tails than a normal distribution.
LOS 5.c
Correlation is a standardized measure of association between two random
variables. It is independent of scale and ranges in value from −1 to +1.

Scatter plots are useful for revealing nonlinear relationships that are not captured
by correlation.
Correlation does not imply that changes in one variable cause changes in the
other. Spurious correlation may result from chance, or from two variables being
related to a third variable.
LOS 5.d
The coefficient of variation is the ratio of the standard deviation of the sample to
its mean and is used to compare the risk-return tradeoffs among distributions of
returns.
Semideviation and target downside deviation are measures of downside risk that
do not include deviations above a given value.
